query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, conformal interfacial layer (for example, a Ni coating applied via atomic layer deposition or sputtering) on the tungsten particles prior to copper infiltration will enhance Cu wettability and interface bonding, thereby reducing void formation and phase separation while preserving mechanical integrity (even under irradiation) compared to conventional vapor-coated W powders.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or connected W regions embedded within a Cu matrix produced by either powder consolidation or vapor coating methods that typically exhibit phase separation and voids limiting thermal transport.
generation.intervention: A single-step deposition of a nanoscale Ni (or similar wetting-promoting refractory) layer on the surfaces of W particles before Cu filling and subsequent sintering.
generation.conditions: The coating process is carried out at low temperature to avoid alteration of the W microstructure, followed by sintering under controlled temperatures below the melting point of W but high enough to allow Cu infiltration and interdiffusion. The processing and subsequent service conditions mimic fusion-reactor joint environments, including irradiation exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous Ni interlayer at the W–Cu interface that acts as a diffusion bridge, reducing interfacial energy and minimizing defects such as voids and segregated phases.
generation.mechanism: The Ni layer improves wettability and promotes uniform bonding between W and Cu by reducing the mismatch in surface energies and enabling controlled interdiffusion during sintering. This creates a graded interface that minimizes deleterious phase separation and void formation, thereby preserving mechanical durability and thermal conductivity during high-temperature and irradiation service.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline of vapor-coated W powders sintered into Cu matrices, the Ni-coated W composite will exhibit a more uniform and defect‐free interfacial microstructure, leading to enhanced thermal transport and mechanical stability under irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints.
generation.baseline: Existing fabrication methods such as spark-plasma sintering of vapor-coated W powders or mechanical alloying of elemental powders, which often yield defects like voids, phase separation, or heterogeneous structures.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable in fusion-reactor components where processing temperatures remain below tungsten's melting point (~3422 °C) and under irradiation conditions up to a few displacements-per-atom (dpa) as encountered in reactor joints. The used Ni layer must remain stable within the operational irradiation and thermal environment.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal thickness of the Ni coating and its long-term stability under neutron and ion irradiation as well as its possible interactions with the Cu matrix over prolonged service times.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite specimens: one set with a thin Ni interlayer deposited on W particles (via atomic layer deposition or sputtering) and one set without the interlayer (using conventional vapor coating). Both sets undergo identical sintering processes and are subsequently exposed to simulated fusion-reactor conditions including high temperature and controlled irradiation (e.g., Ar+, He+, and D+ ion beams) to mimic service conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM and EDS mapping) to quantify interfacial uniformity, void fraction, and phase separation.
Thermal conductivity measurements to assess improvements in heat transport.
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., nanoindentation, flexural strength) before and after irradiation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in voids and phase separation, nor improvements in thermal conductivity and mechanical properties under irradiation compared to the uncoated baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A powder metallurgical technique using elemental powder mixing has been exploited by developing and analyzing a novel high-entropy alloy (WxTaTiVCr, simplified as xWs) and its derivative alloys for the development of reduced-activation alloys for future fusion power plants. Various compositions realized by varying the W content from 32 to 90at.% with in-situ TiC were prepared by consolidating a powder mixture through spark plasma sintering at 1600 °C. The relative density of the alloys sintered at 1600 °C was found to increase with a decrease in the W content. The characterization of xWs samples by XRD showed the BCC crystal structure of the alloys. A microstructural examination by SEM-EDS revealed multiple phases in the microstructures as bright, gray and dark regions. Moreover, various W-rich phases were observed in the matrix of the sintered samples. An investigation of these phases under TEM and a selected-area diffraction pattern analysis disclosed the presence of TiC in the W-rich matrix, as observed in BSE images.
